questions.q: Why does the lesson say a business goal like 'reduce support costs by 20% via higher AI deflection' is not yet an engineering plan?
options: It contains zero technical specifics -- turning it into specific, sequenced technical initiatives is the engineer's job, not something leadership hands down already specified
Business goals are always too vague to ever be actionable
This particular goal is factually impossible to achieve
Engineering plans and business goals are the exact same kind of document
questions.explain: The goal states a desired OUTCOME with no technical mechanism specified -- breaking it into concrete, sequenced initiatives is the translation work a Staff/Principal engineer is expected to do.

questions.q: Why does the refactor initiative (Lesson 18) belong on the roadmap even though leadership never asked for it and it doesn't directly move the deflection-rate metric?
options: It's a real, identified dependency for the hybrid-search initiative that DOES move the metric -- building on top of the current duplicated logic would mean implementing hybrid search five times instead of once
All technical debt should always be refactored regardless of any business goal
The refactor was actually requested by leadership but just wasn't mentioned in the business goal
Roadmaps should never include any item that doesn't directly move the headline metric
questions.explain: A roadmap that only lists metric-moving items without surfacing real dependencies risks discovering blockers mid-quarter -- the refactor is on the roadmap because it genuinely unblocks other planned work.

questions.q: Why does the lesson call sequencing 'the hardest and most valuable part' of roadmapping, as distinct from simply listing initiatives?
options: Figuring out what genuinely has to happen before what prevents wasted work (building on a foundation about to be refactored) and false assumptions that unrelated work can all start simultaneously
Sequencing is actually the easiest part of roadmapping, not the hardest
Listing initiatives and sequencing them are identical tasks with no real difference
Sequencing only matters for roadmaps with fewer than three initiatives
questions.explain: Listing WHAT needs to happen is relatively straightforward; reasoning about dependencies (what blocks what) is where real planning risk and value lie, as shown by the refactor-before-hybrid-search example.

questions.q: How does Lesson 3's capacity planning feed into this roadmap, according to the lesson?
options: It tells the team whether expanding the knowledge base (initiative 2) will push infrastructure past a capacity ceiling partway through the year, which changes how that initiative should be sequenced
Capacity planning has no real connection to roadmapping decisions
Capacity planning only applies to decisions about vector databases, never to knowledge-base expansion
Capacity planning replaces the need for any roadmap sequencing at all
questions.explain: This is a direct example of the lesson's closing point -- earlier course tools (like capacity forecasting) become concrete inputs into how a real roadmap gets sequenced, not separate, unrelated skills.

questions.q: What is the lesson's overall point about how roadmapping relates to the rest of this course?
options: Roadmapping isn't a separate skill learned from scratch -- it's where tools like capacity planning, build-vs-buy, and tech-debt break-even math from earlier lessons get applied together under one real business goal
Roadmapping is a completely unrelated skill with no connection to anything covered earlier in the course
Roadmapping only requires knowledge of business strategy, with no technical skills involved
Roadmapping replaces the need to ever write a design document or ADR
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly shows capacity planning, build-vs-buy, and tech-debt economics all feeding into this one roadmap -- roadmapping is presented as an integration point for the course's other skills, not a standalone topic.
